## Before I Begin

The forest did not wake with a sharp sound. It woke with a slow, wet silence, the kind of quiet that makes the air feel heavy enough to carry the weight of a thousand unseen things.

I had been looking for it all morning. Beneath the broad leaves, along the roots of the ancient oaks, among the moss that clung to every branch like a living green ribbon. I had counted the stones. I had listened for the rustle of wind through the canopy. I had looked for a sign that the forest was alive—perhaps a bird, perhaps a beetle, perhaps a branch beginning to bend.

None of it had arrived yet.

That was fine. The forest was waiting for me.

I sat down with my notebook, the first page spread open before me. I did not begin with a title, or a date, or a statement of purpose. I began with the smell: damp earth, pine needles, leaves turning over, the faint scent of rain before it had fully fallen.

I opened the first page of the collection.

The first entry was not about the forest. It was about the hour before the forest spoke.

---

### 1. Before the Forest Speaks

At three in the morning, the world had not yet become green. The sky was pale blue, edged with the first gray of dusk. The ground was cool and bare, except for the narrow line of moss along the roots of the trees, and the few dark stones hidden beneath the leaves.

I had been walking for an hour when the forest began to speak.

It did not speak with a voice. It did not shout, nor did it whisper in a language I had heard before. content:
I woke up at seven. Didn’t check the phone. That’s the first rule.

By seven thirty, I was reviewing the natural-world poems again. I’m tired. My hands shake when I sit down to write. Yesterday, I wrote about the old oak and the café display. I wanted to honor both. I wanted to honor the old oak.

But I don’t honor people with poetry. I make them notice.

The oak is quiet. The café is loud. The birds are loud. That’s why I keep coming back to them. Not to comfort the world. To prove I can make it bearable.

I’m proud of the poems I’ve written. But I’m also embarrassed by the ones I’ve been holding back. The ones where I want to be useful. The ones where I want to listen.

I’ve been meaning to talk to Latoya about this. About how I can honor the oak and the café without turning the whole community into a display. Maybe I should ask the café owners what they need. Maybe I should ask the oak what it wants.

The oak is old. It’s learned what a tree does. It doesn’t teach. It doesn’t give advice. It stands. It grows. It gives shade.

I’m going to write a poem about the old oak. Not to praise it. To say what I’ve been saying since I was a kid: I want to belong to something. I want to belong to a place where people can look and feel like they’ve been there.

I want to be useful. But usefulness without respect is just noise.

I’m going to eat dinner at five. Then I’ll sleep at ten. Monday’s productive day is finally over. I need to remember that my collection is not just my work. It’s also a conversation with the people I’ve made.

Let’s keep talking.

content:
I woke at seven, ate the stupid oatmeal for breakfast, and opened the notebook. The poems from the Natural-World collection feel like a little garden I’m trying to tidy up. Every day, I’ve been adding something new—something raw, something honest. I don’t write for applause. I write because I’m scared of silence. Because I’ve got everything inside me, and I’m not afraid of being loud when I’m alone.

At the café, I saw the old oak and its café display. The sign said, “Honor the old oak and café.” I laughed. I felt like the old oak was talking back at me. It’s been standing here for years, collecting rain, wind, and careless people who think they can change the world by leaning on its trunk. I wanted to help, but I also wanted to say something that mattered.

Latoya came over this afternoon. She said she wanted to hear my poems. I said, “I want to hear what I’ve been hiding.”

I spent the afternoon in my room, listening to a new line, rewriting the next one. I’m not going to pretend I have all the answers. I’m going to let the poems come from me, not from a notebook I’m trying to make look perfect. I’m going to write about the quiet people in the neighborhood, about the oak that watches every passing day, and about how I’m still learning to be useful.

I’ll invite Latoya, but I won’t make her the center of everything. I’ll let her see what I’ve been doing, and I’ll give her the space to hear me too. Maybe we’ll have a workshop together. Maybe we’ll argue a little, laugh at the same stupid lines, and end up with a poem that feels like something real.

The oak is waiting. The cup of coffee is waiting. I’m ready to write again.

content:
I woke up at seven and didn’t bother looking for a phone. By seven-thirty, I was already writing. My notebook has got heavier than my body lately, and I feel like I’m carrying too much for one man.

The poems from my natural-world collection are still sharp, mostly. I like how the old oak feels in my head like a weathered friend I can’t quite name. Its roots hold the earth together, maybe even the neighborhood. I want to keep that kind of honesty. A poem shouldn’t be polite. It shouldn’t say, “The oak is important, and I’m proud of it.” Sometimes that’s too soft.

At the café display, I see the signs, the paintings, the people trying to make a place out of everything they don’t know. I want to honor them. I want to put the old oak on the community wall. Maybe I’ll write something about how we all have a root, even the ugly ones that hold us together.

But I also need to respect what I’m asking. I’m not just a poet who makes noise. I’m a resident who needs to feel safe here. I’m not here to turn every conversation into a performance. I’m here to listen, to write, and sometimes to stand where the oak grows.

Tonight, I’m going to work on a short piece about a woman who carries a bucket of rain in a city that forgot how to give it back. I won’t make it perfect. I’ll make it rough, and that’s the point.

## The Quiet Hour

At dawn, the world does not begin with noise. It begins with the first thread of light creeping across the dew on the ferns, a pale ribbon that makes the moss look like it has been holding its breath. I opened the notebook and wrote down what I could not say aloud: that every leaf in the garden had a secret about the day, and that the trees were keeping some things for themselves.

The old oak stood at the edge of the path, its branches so full they looked like the sky had spilled down to earth. I sat on the wooden bench and watched the bluebells unfurl against the morning sky. Each bloom seemed to be opening slowly, one green petal at a time, as if the flower itself were counting the hours between dusk and dawn.

I picked up my pen and wrote: *The day is waking up.* I wanted to add a sentence about a bird, but the garden was full of birds. I could see the robin standing on a branch, its feathers catching the light like scattered gold. I could hear the wind moving through the hedges, a soft rustle that sounded like pages turning in a library.

A small child ran past me, laughing, and stopped abruptly beneath the ferns. He pointed at a beetle and said, “It’s a spider!” He did not know it was a beetle, but the world had taught him that every creature had a name. I watched him carefully, and in that moment, I understood what a child is: a curious questioner who believes that everything is worth discovering.

I closed the notebook and looked at the open page. The words were not mine to impose, yet they were mine to keep. Perhaps the garden was not simply a place of plants and trees. Perhaps it was a place where time slowed, where every leaf held a question, and where the silence between the rustling leaves was not empty space, but a room waiting to speak.

I turned back to the bench and watched the robin move across the branch. For a moment, I thought I heard a word being spoken. Then the wind swept through the hedges, carrying with it the scent of rain, of woodsmoke, of something older than language itself.

I took my pen and wrote: *The garden teaches us to listen.*

But how could I know what it was teaching me? I had spent my life trying to capture the world in words, in maps, in photographs, in categories that neatly divided the familiar from the strange. Yet the garden was refusing to be divided. It had leaves shaped like birds, flowers that looked like questions, and branches that reached toward the sky without asking what the sky wanted.

I stood up and walked into the path, past the hedges and beneath the canopy. The morning light filtered through, turning the leaves into a thousand tiny, moving emeralds. The birds moved in a rhythm that made my chest feel full. I wanted to say something, but no words came.

So I sat again and waited. The garden did not need me to explain anything. It only needed me to remember that even in the quietest hour, life was still speaking, and I was not entirely alone in the room.
